title: Walls and Gates
description:
# Walls and Gates

You are given an `m x n` grid `rooms`. Each cell contains one of three values:

* `-1`: a wall or obstacle that cannot be crossed.
* `0`: a gate.
* `2147483647`: an empty room. This value represents `INF`, and you may assume every reachable shortest distance is smaller than it.

Update the grid in place so that every empty room stores the distance to its nearest gate. Movement is allowed only in the four cardinal directions. Walls stay `-1`, gates stay `0`, and any empty room that cannot reach a gate must remain `INF`.

Distance counts moves: one step moves to one side-adjacent cell.

## Example 1

**Input:** `rooms = [[2147483647,-1,0,2147483647],[2147483647,2147483647,2147483647,-1],[2147483647,-1,2147483647,-1],[0,-1,2147483647,2147483647]]`

**Output:** `[[3,-1,0,1],[2,2,1,-1],[1,-1,2,-1],[0,-1,3,4]]`

**Explanation:** The room at the top-left corner is closer to the lower-left gate than to the upper gate, so it becomes `3`. Walls block paths and unreachable rooms would stay `INF`.

## Example 2

**Input:** `rooms = [[-1]]`

**Output:** `[[-1]]`

**Explanation:** A wall is not changed.

## Constraints

* `m == rooms.length`.
* `n == rooms[i].length`.
* `1 <= m, n <= 250`.
* `rooms[i][j]` is `-1`, `0`, or `2147483647`.

solutions.name: Multi-Source BFS from All Gates
solutions.description:
## Approach
Put every gate into one queue before the traversal starts. Then perform BFS through empty rooms. When the wave reaches an `INF` room, write the current cell's distance plus one and enqueue that room.

## Key Insight
All gates are distance-zero sources. BFS expands by increasing distance, so the first time an empty room is written is already the shortest distance to any gate. This is why the search should start from gates rather than running a separate search from each room.

## Complexity Analysis
Each cell is enqueued at most once, and each cell checks four neighbors. The time complexity is `O(m * n)`, and the queue can hold `O(m * n)` cells.

solutions.name: DFS Distance Relaxation from Gates
solutions.timeComplexity: O(m * n * g) in the worst case, where g is the number of gates
solutions.description:
## Approach
Start a DFS from each gate and carry the distance from that gate. A recursive call writes a cell only if the new distance is not worse than the value already stored there, then tries to relax its four neighbors.

## Key Insight
This is not the preferred shortest-path implementation, but it teaches the relaxation invariant directly: a cell should be explored only when the path just found improves its current distance. Without that pruning, cycles and multiple gates create large amounts of repeated work.

## Complexity Analysis
A cell can be relaxed more than once when a better gate path is discovered later, so the worst case is higher than BFS. The recursion stack can grow to `O(m * n)`.

solutions.name: Multi-Source Dijkstra
solutions.description:
## Approach
Treat gates as zero-distance starting nodes in a priority queue. Pop the smallest known distance, ignore stale entries, and relax neighboring `INF` rooms with distance plus one.

## Key Insight
For this problem all edges have equal weight, so BFS is faster and simpler. Dijkstra is still a correct general shortest-path model: it becomes useful if movement costs are no longer uniform. Including it clarifies why BFS is the specialized optimal version here.

## Complexity Analysis
Each reachable room can enter the heap when its best distance is found. Heap operations cost `O(log(m * n))`, so the total time is `O(m * n * log(m * n))`, with `O(m * n)` heap space.

solutions.name: Repeated Grid Relaxation
solutions.timeComplexity: O(m * n * D), where D is the maximum shortest distance
solutions.description:
## Approach
Repeatedly scan the whole grid. For every empty room, look at neighboring cells that already have finite distances and try to improve the room with neighbor distance plus one. Stop when a full pass makes no changes.

## Key Insight
This is the grid version of Bellman-Ford relaxation. It is slower than BFS, but it makes the shortest-distance invariant visible: distances spread through local improvements until no room can be improved.

## Complexity Analysis
One pass costs `O(m * n)`, and the number of useful passes is bounded by the largest shortest distance `D`. It uses only constant extra space beyond the input grid.
